analysis.one_liner: Criminalizes private equity practices that harm patients at health care firms they acquire.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee; no hearing, no vote, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime, punishable by one to six years in prison, for private equity executives whose actions contribute to a hospital or nursing home closing, missing payroll, defaulting on loans, or going bankrupt in a way that injures or kills patients. It would let the Justice Department and state attorneys general claw back up to ten years of executive pay, fees, and profits from such deals, with the money going to unpaid workers and harmed communities. It would also cut off Medicare and Medicaid payments to providers that sell their buildings to real estate investment trusts, repeal tax benefits those trusts get on health care property, require large health care entities to publicly report their ownership, debt, and fees to investors, and order a federal study of profit-driven practices in health care.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients at hospitals, nursing homes, hospices, and physician practices owned by private equity or other investment funds would get a new layer of protection: executives who take money out and then oversee a collapse that harms patients could face prison and lose up to a decade of compensation, with recovered funds going to unpaid pensions, wages, and community health needs. Health care workers would be protected through the clawback fund for salary and pension shortfalls. Medicare and Medicaid taxpayers would benefit from the ban on paying providers that sell assets to REITs, and the public would gain visibility into who owns and profits from health care entities through the annual reporting requirement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and workers at investment-owned health facilities

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new federal crime (one to six years in prison) for private equity firms or other covered parties whose actions contribute to a triggering event — closure, 90+ days of unpaid rent or loan default, missing payroll for over a quarter of the workforce, or bankruptcy — that injures or kills a patient at the acquired health care organization.

Authorizes the Attorney General and state attorneys general to claw back covered compensation — salaries, bonuses, management and monitoring fees, proceeds from asset sales, severance, and golden parachutes — received during the ten years before or after a triggering event, with an affirmative defense only if the firm proves by clear and convincing evidence it could not prevent the event.

Directs clawed-back money to cover shortfalls in salaries, benefits, and pension funds of harmed employees, and to serve the health care needs of the harmed community, with pension shortfalls prioritized when bankruptcy is the triggering event.

Prohibits entities from receiving Medicare and Medicaid payments if they sell assets to, or pledge assets as collateral with, a real estate investment trust, and repeals the special tax rules that let REITs earn favorable treatment on health care property and deduct qualified REIT dividends from qualified business income.

Requires hospitals, health systems, physician practices, nursing homes, hospices, dialysis facilities, and similar entities to report annually on ownership, control, debt, real estate leases, fees and dividends paid to investors, with the information posted on a public HHS website starting in 2027, backed by civil penalties up to $5 million for false or missing reports.

Orders the HHS Inspector General to study profit-driven practices in health care — including up-coding, staffing reductions, prior authorization restrictions by insurers, and efforts by private equity to evade state corporate practice of medicine laws — and estimate the financial returns accruing to investors.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity firms, their executives and control persons, and other investment funds that acquire health care companies would face new criminal exposure, clawbacks of up to ten years of compensation, and civil penalties up to five times any clawback. Health care REITs would lose the Medicare/Medicaid revenue stream from provider-landlord arrangements and would lose favorable tax treatment on health care property and REIT dividends. Large health care entities would bear the cost of annual ownership and financial reporting. Some facilities that rely on REIT sale-leaseback financing could face harder access to capital.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity firms and health care REITs

drawbacks.text: The bill's definitions are sweeping: 'covered compensation' includes any profits from buying or selling assets, and 'control person' reaches shareholders, directors, and operators with as little as 10 percent ownership, so the threat of prison could chill investment in struggling hospitals and nursing homes that some investors currently keep open — facilities that might otherwise close outright.

Cutting off Medicare and Medicaid payments to providers that sell assets to REITs, rather than regulating the terms of those deals, could leave some facilities without financing options, since sale-leaseback deals with REITs are a common source of capital for nursing homes and hospitals.
Aggressive clawbacks and criminal exposure for executives could raise the cost of capital for health care acquisitions generally, which could slow deals that bring money into underfunded facilities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a documented pattern — investment firms loading acquired health care companies with debt, fees, and sale-leaseback deals, then walking away when the company fails, with patients and workers absorbing the damage. The core protections (criminal liability tied to actual patient harm, clawbacks that fund unpaid wages and pensions, transparency reporting) are aimed narrowly at that pattern, with an affirmative defense for firms that could not have prevented the event. The REIT payment ban is blunter: it cuts off the entire arrangement rather than policing its terms, and could squeeze capital for facilities that need it. On balance, the benefits for patients and workers are large and direct; the main costs fall on investors whose business model the bill is deliberately designed to make unprofitable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on June 11, 2024, with Senator Edward Markey as the second sponsor.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance; the full action history shows no further action — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote.
It had two cosponsors, both Democrats, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity firms and health care REITs are better off: none of the penalties, clawbacks, payment bans, or tax changes took effect, and executives remain free to use the same deal structures. Patients and workers at investment-owned facilities gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity firms and health care REITs

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assigned it its criminal clawback, REIT payment ban, tax, and transparency provisions.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Private equity and health care real estate industry
against.role: Industries the bill would penalize and tax
against.what_they_did: The industries targeted by the bill have publicly campaigned against similar private equity health care restrictions in Congress and state legislatures, and no senator outside the two sponsors publicly backed this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All three senators involved — the sponsor and two cosponsors — were Democrats, and the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee took no action; no Republican supported the bill.

industries.industry: Private equity firms and investment companies
industries.note: The bill would create prison terms of one to six years and civil penalties up to five times clawed-back compensation for PE executives whose actions contribute to a triggering event that injures or kills a patient, and would claw back a decade of fees, bonuses, and asset-sale profits. Its core design is to make extracting money from health care companies and leaving patients harmed unprofitable.

industries.industry: Health care real estate investment trusts (REITs)
industries.note: REITs profit by buying provider buildings and leasing them back at rents paid from Medicare and Medicaid revenue. The bill would cut off federal health payments to providers that sell assets to REITs and repeal the tax benefits REITs get on health care property and REIT dividends, striking at the sale-leaseback model.

industries.industry: Hospitals, nursing homes, and physician practices owned by investment firms
industries.note: These facilities would face annual public reporting of ownership, debt, and investor fees, and their landlords' REIT arrangements could lose federal payment eligibility — but the same operators would face accountability when cost-cutting harms patients, and clawed-back funds would cover their unpaid wages and pensions.

industries.industry: Private insurers and corporate health care entities
industries.note: The bill's transparency rules would expose ownership and revenue-sharing arrangements across the health care sector, and the ordered Inspector General study would examine insurer practices like prior authorization restrictions and evasion of state corporate practice of medicine laws, increasing scrutiny of how these entities profit.
